video_title: Does The Jobs Report Change Anything?
gist: Ed Yardeni argues the weak July payroll report is a seasonal/demographic mirage — the labor market is tight at 4.1% unemployment because supply fell faster than demand — so the Fed still has an inflation problem (GDP deflator 4.3%, core 3.8%) and should be biased toward hiking, not cutting. He stays bullish on an earnings-led ('FIMO', not FOMO) bull market with a 10,000 S&P 500 year-end target, while flagging that the real tail risk has shifted from a 2000-style valuation bubble to a 2008-style credit event in AI/hyperscaler financing. (Speaker opens the session dating it 'Monday, August 10th,' earlier than the listed upload date.)

themes.theme: Jobs report: weak headline, tight labor market

insights.claim: The weak July payroll print does not change the macro picture because labor supply fell faster than labor demand, pushing unemployment down to 4.1% — a balanced, full-employment labor market rather than a deteriorating one.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Positioning for imminent Fed easing on 'weak jobs' is the wrong read; watch the unemployment rate, not the payroll headline.
insights.quote: we think on on unbalanced the labor market is balanced and uh that uh supply equals demand and at full employment with the unemployment rate now actually down to 4.1%

insights.claim: The shrinking labor force is structural, not cyclical noise: retiring baby boomers, stricter immigration enforcement, and skills mismatches are the three drivers, with boomer retirement the largest.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A structurally shrinking labor supply keeps wage pressure and the unemployment rate low even with anemic job growth — a persistently hawkish input for the Fed.
insights.quote: the labor force decline isn't some kind of random event. It's related to the retiring baby boomers. It's related to stricter migration uh and it's also related to skills skills mismatches

insights.claim: The payroll weakness is concentrated in state and local government education, which Yardeni attributes to a seasonal-adjustment artifact he expects to reverse in the August report.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Anyone trading the next payroll print should expect a mechanical government-education rebound to flatter the August number.

insights.claim: Two consecutive months of leisure and hospitality job losses reflect World Cup staffing that was front-loaded into April–May and is now being unwound, not underlying consumer weakness.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Discount the leisure/hospitality drag when assessing consumer-facing equities and the services economy.

insights.claim: The six-month average of payroll gains is running around 44,000 per month, inside the 40,000–60,000 breakeven range needed to hold the unemployment rate steady given demographics.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Breakeven job growth has collapsed, so prints that look recessionary by pre-pandemic standards are actually neutral — reset the recession trigger level.
insights.quote: the six-month average is like earning around 44,000 per month, which uh I think most economists agree is probably close to the break even. Break even maybe being 40 to 60,000

insights.claim: Under-the-hood labor detail is constructive: construction employment is at an all-time record high, manufacturing is adding jobs, the payroll diffusion index shows slightly more than half of companies hiring, layoffs are extremely low, and short-duration (under five weeks) unemployment is falling.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Breadth internals argue against a labor-market cliff; fading recession trades on the headline print has statistical support.

insights.claim: Information technology employment is falling because the sector over-hired during the pandemic and is now compressing headcount with AI, but IT pay increases remain decent — a productivity story rather than a demand-collapse story.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Tech job losses should be read as margin-positive, not as a leading recession signal.

insights.claim: Seniors 65 and older now make up roughly 50% of everyone not in the labor force, and the 55+ and 65+ participation rates are both edging lower as the largest, longest-living cohort exits.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Participation-rate declines will be misread as slack for years; they are demographic and won't reverse with easier policy.

insights.claim: Foreign-born labor force growth is declining while native-born growth is rising, and because foreign-born workers have a higher participation rate, deportations and self-deportation mechanically drag down the aggregate participation rate.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Immigration enforcement is an ongoing supply-side tightener for wages — a structural inflation input separate from tariffs.

themes.theme: Fed: the case for hiking, not cutting

insights.claim: Yardeni explicitly endorses the view that the latest labor data strengthens the case for a Fed rate HIKE, because falling supply amid demographics, reduced immigration, and AI-driven skills mismatch makes the labor market tighter and will boost inflationary wage pressures.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni (agreeing with viewer 'William/Villim')
insights.so_what: A hike-bias view against a consensus expecting cuts — bearish for front-end rates and for duration-sensitive equity factors if it gains traction.
insights.quote: I would argue that the latest US labor market data strengthened the case for a Fed rate hike because the labor market has gotten more tight. I agree.

insights.claim: Inflation remains the Fed's actual problem: the overall GDP deflator is running 4.3% and the ex-food-and-energy measure 3.8%, nowhere near the 2% target.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: If the Fed is anchored to deflator-based measures rather than the labor market, the easing path priced into rates is too aggressive.
insights.quote: we're looking at the GDP deflator is for the overall economy is 43 excluding food and energy is 3.8. These are not close to 2%.

insights.claim: The Fed faces a repeat of the transitory debate: tariffs, oil, and Middle East supply-chain disruptions are the current shocks, and the open question is whether second- and third-round effects force a response.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Frame each new inflation shock by asking whether it propagates — that's the variable that flips the Fed from patient to reactive.

insights.claim: Yardeni maintains the Fed made a mistake with its 2024 policy decision and says the bond market has since confirmed he was right and the Fed was wrong.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A track-record claim that underpins his hawkish stance; watch long-end yields as the arbiter of Fed credibility.

insights.claim: Unit labor cost inflation should be a strong disinflationary force over time given underlying productivity and compensation trends, but interim supply shocks are overwhelming it.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: The structural disinflation case rests on productivity, so productivity data is the key release for the medium-term inflation path.

themes.theme: AI capex as a credit event, not a valuation bubble

insights.claim: The relevant analogy for AI risk is 2008 (a credit event) rather than 2000 (a valuation/FOMO event), because a lot of debt is now being raised to finance AI buildout.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Monitor AI-linked credit spreads and issuance, not just tech multiples, for the signal that the cycle is turning.
insights.quote: There's some debate now about well if this is not 2000, could this be 2008? Uh 2000 was uh FOMO in the technology sector. 2008 was uh irrational exuberance in home prices and uh creating all sorts of credit derivatives.

insights.claim: Recessions are almost always caused by credit bubbles bursting into credit crunches — Yardeni's core recession framework, which he notes applied even to 2000 via telecom vendor financing funded by hundreds of billions in junk bond issuance.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Use credit conditions, not GDP or payrolls, as the primary recession early-warning system; vendor financing is the historical tell.
insights.quote: one of the conclusions I've come to studying recessions over the years is that more often than not, almost always they're caused by uh the credit bubbles uh that burst, which then leads to credit crunches

insights.claim: The speed at which hyperscalers flipped from large free cash flow to negative free cash flow and became borrowers, combined with circular dependencies among them, is the most unsettling feature of the AI trade.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Track hyperscaler FCF and debt issuance directly — the balance-sheet turn, not the revenue line, is where the risk accumulates.
insights.quote: it is uh somewhat unsettling how quickly uh these hyperscalers went from lots of free cash flow to negative cash flow uh free cash flow and now have to borrow money

insights.claim: Strong cloud revenues and backlogs are the bull counterargument, but digging into them reveals circularity and customer concentration issues that undercut their signal value.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Discount reported AI backlog growth where counterparties are also suppliers or equity-linked partners.

insights.claim: Nobody knows where AI is heading — winners and losers are genuinely undetermined — and Yardeni's firm sees nothing about to burst right now, keeping a stay-objective rather than call-the-top posture.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Even a structural bull has no conviction on AI winners — argues for breadth/index exposure over concentrated AI single-name bets.
insights.quote: nobody really knows where this is all heading. There's a lot of uncertainties with regards to uh uh who the winners are, who who the losers are now that a lot of debt is being raised to finance this

insights.claim: Hyperscalers get 100% depreciation from the outset, which saves substantial tax and helps free cash flow, but they are spending so fast that free cash flow stays negative anyway.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni (answering viewer 'Amy')
insights.so_what: The coming depreciation-expense drag on reported hyperscaler earnings is partly offset by tax treatment — but doesn't rescue cash flow.

themes.theme: Earnings-led bull market and the FIMO framework

insights.claim: This bull market is driven by 'FIMO' — fabulous earnings momentum — not FOMO, with the forward P/E flat around 20 rather than expanding.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: If the rally is earnings-driven, the kill switch is an earnings-estimate reset, not a multiple de-rating — watch revisions, not valuation.
insights.quote: FIMO fabulous earnings momentum is what's driven this market up not FOMO

insights.claim: The reported forward P/E has fallen to about 19, but only because mark-to-market capital gains at Amazon and Google inflated 'other income' in earnings; stripping those out puts the true forward P/E back at roughly 20.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Screened index valuation is currently flattered by non-operating gains — adjust before concluding the market got cheaper.

insights.claim: Semiconductors now trade below the market multiple and technology roughly at the market multiple, which Yardeni says makes the current setup structurally different from 1999–2000.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: The 'tech is a bubble on valuation' argument doesn't hold on relative multiples — bears need an earnings argument instead.

insights.claim: The real risk of irrational exuberance has migrated from valuations to earnings expectations themselves — the market may be in an earnings bubble rather than a P/E bubble.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: The most under-hedged exposure is to consensus EPS estimates, particularly semiconductor estimates tied to the AI trade.
insights.quote: while we may not have uh irrational exuberance on the FOMO side, on the PE side, could it be that we have irrational exuberance on the and the on the earnings side?

insights.claim: Yardeni identifies the specific trigger for a market problem as an event on the AI trade that forces investors to reconsider semiconductor earnings estimates — and says we are not there yet.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A concrete, monitorable kill-switch: the first credible AI-demand disappointment that cascades into semi estimate cuts.
insights.quote: If we suddenly get something happening on the AI trade that makes everybody kind of reconsider their earnings estimates for semiconductors and so on. Uh that would be a problem, but I don't think we're there yet.

insights.claim: The 2027 EPS estimate keeps rising and is cleaner than 2026 because analysts do not model future mark-to-market capital gains into spreadsheets — so as forward earnings converge toward 2027, the earnings base becomes less polluted.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: The forward-earnings roll into 2027 is a mechanical tailwind to the index target math over the next few months.
insights.quote: I don't think analysts are marking into their Excel spreadsheet capital gains uh on um additional capital gains. They'll take them as they happen.

insights.claim: The mark-to-market capital gains at just a couple of the Magnificent 7 are so large that Yardeni had to rescale his chart; stripping them out puts sector growth back near the ~22% and ~27% pace seen in the next two quarters, with the pops concentrated in communication services and consumer discretionary (Amazon), while tech's growth has been steady without capital-gain distortion.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Sector earnings-growth screens for comm services and consumer discretionary are currently distorted by one-off investment gains.

insights.claim: 20% year-over-year earnings growth is not sustainable because earnings cannot grow faster than nominal GDP indefinitely, against a 7–8% historical norm.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni (answering viewer 'Gary')
insights.so_what: Build in earnings-growth mean reversion when extrapolating index targets beyond the next few quarters.
insights.quote: 20% year-over-year uh earnings growth is not sustainable. Earnings growth historically has been 7 to 8%. You you can't have earnings growing sustainably faster than the nominal GDP.

insights.claim: Profit margins have stopped being cyclical and have been trending structurally higher for several years, which along with strong revenues and a resilient global economy explains the above-trend earnings growth.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A secular margin uptrend justifies a higher sustainable P/E and undercuts classic mean-reversion bear cases.
insights.quote: Profit margin just is no longer cyclical. It's been actually uh trending higher for the past several years.

insights.claim: Yardeni keeps a 10,000 year-end S&P 500 target with the index near 7,800, while separately noting that applying a 20x multiple to his 2027 EPS figure yields over 8,000 — two different anchors for the same year-end.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: An explicit, testable bull target implying substantial further upside; note the internal gap between the headline target and the multiple-based math.
insights.quote: we got 10,000 still on the S&P 500 by year end. And doesn't look like such a crazy forecast with the S&P at almost 7,800 now.

themes.theme: Market breadth and the 1985 melt-up analog

insights.claim: Market breadth is confirming the rally: the equal-weight and cap-weighted S&P 500 are both at record highs, and the 'impressive 493' has outperformed the Magnificent 7 recently.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Breadth expansion argues for equal-weight exposure over mega-cap concentration and reduces the odds of an imminent top.

insights.claim: The Russell 2000 at an all-time record high is a key non-signal: small caps normally lead in flagging rising recession or credit risk, and they are not doing so.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Use small-cap relative performance as the real-time credit-stress gauge for the AI-debt thesis; it is currently clean.
insights.quote: usually the small caps will be the first indicators that the recession is risk is increasing or credit risk is increasing and the Russell 2000 is an all-time record high

insights.claim: Lining up the S&P 500 since 2015 against 1985 produces a tracking analog suggesting a possible melt-up and substantial further upside, though Yardeni concedes the alignment was adjusted to fit and prefers a sustainable bull market to a melt-up.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A melt-up-then-bust path is live in the bull case, which changes optimal exit timing versus a steady-grind scenario.
insights.quote: we obviously jiggled around until we got this thing to look right

insights.claim: Placed against bull markets since 1966, the current advance sits mid-pack in duration and magnitude, consistent with the 'Roaring 2020s' thesis running through the end of the decade.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Historical bull-market distribution gives no age-based reason to de-risk yet.

themes.theme: Gold, the dollar, and Fed credibility

insights.claim: Yardeni maintains his upside call on gold: $4,000 has held and formed a base, with the price now around $4,400 after a fast move.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: $4,000 is the stated technical base to trade against for anyone sizing gold exposure.
insights.quote: especially now that it looks like 4,000 held uh we formed a nice base of 4,000. Uh last I looked we were about 4,400. That's a a nice big move in a very short period of time.

insights.claim: Gold's rally is being driven by a Fed credibility problem rather than war risk — gold did poorly while the Middle East conflict was kinetic, and rose after Warsh talked tough on price stability in June and July but did nothing, saying the Fed is 'not on pause' but merely 'studying everything.'
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Gold here is a short-central-bank-credibility trade, so it can keep rising even if geopolitics calm — and would reverse on an actual hawkish action.
insights.quote: there's some I think it kind of reflects a little bit of a credibility issue on uh on Wars

insights.claim: The US Treasury intervened alongside Japan's Ministry of Finance to support the yen, using euros without asking the Europeans, because the MOF's alternative was selling from its roughly $1 trillion of US Treasuries — an outcome Scott Bessent does not want on his watch.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
entities: Bank of Japan / Ministry of Finance
insights.so_what: Yen weakness is now a direct US rates risk; the intervention reveals Treasury's pain threshold and adds a policy bid under gold.
insights.quote: the ministry of finance finance to support the yen could always sell their trillion dollars some of their trillion dollars of US treasuries to to to provide that uh that that kind of support

themes.theme: Consumer wealth and the G-shaped economy

insights.claim: The silent generation plus baby boomers hold roughly $110 trillion of net worth — an unprecedented concentration of wealth among seniors that supports spending even as earned income stagnates.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Consumption is increasingly wealth-funded rather than wage-funded — bullish for senior-skewed discretionary spending and asset-price-sensitive demand.
insights.quote: taking the silent generation and the baby boomers and you're talking about $ 110 trillion of net worth for seniors

insights.claim: The savings rate is falling and will likely turn negative, which bears will call unsustainable — but Yardeni reframes it as evidence of a 'G-shaped' (generational, senior-wealth-driven) economy rather than a 'K-shaped' one.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A negative savings rate print is a coming bear headline that Yardeni argues should be faded, not traded on.
insights.quote: And we'll tell you that's that's the G-shaped economy, not the K-shaped economy.

insights.claim: Average hourly earnings understate wage strength because they are not composition-adjusted: high-paid boomers exiting the workforce shifts weight toward lower-wage workers, mechanically dragging the series down — the mirror image of the pandemic-era distortion when low-wage workers lost jobs.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Cooling AHE is not evidence of cooling wage inflation; use composition-adjusted wage trackers before concluding the Fed can ease.
insights.quote: average hourly earnings is not one of the better measures of wages because it's not adjusted for composition

insights.claim: Wage growth by sector shows utilities leading at 8.1%, construction and natural resources at 4.4%, and manufacturing at 3.8%, with Yardeni linking some of the strength to the AI boom.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Utilities wage inflation is a real-economy fingerprint of AI datacenter demand — a cross-check on the AI capex cycle's persistence.
insights.quote: utilities are doing extremely well at 8.1%. Again some of these can be related to the ai boom.

insights.claim: Yardeni's earned income proxy was roughly flat in July and he expects disposable personal income to be flat again, but attributes it to boomer retirement rather than consumer distress.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Flat income prints will be misread as consumer weakness; the offsetting wealth effect is the variable that matters.

themes.theme: Middle East, oil, and the Hormuz disruption

insights.claim: Yardeni's revised view is that the Iran conflict will be protracted rather than quickly resolved, because the country is effectively run by the IRGC — a jihadist organization he argues cannot be negotiated or compromised with — reversing his day-one conclusion after the regime decapitation.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Price a persistent geopolitical risk premium in oil rather than fading each escalation as a short-lived spike.

insights.claim: The Strait of Hormuz is still not free for navigation and continues to disrupt oil supplies, with oil prices up on the latest Middle East developments, while Trump shifts toward sanctions and an economic blockade of Iran rather than imminent strikes.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Ongoing Hormuz supply disruption is a live inflation shock feeding the Fed's problem — an energy-inflation hedge remains relevant.
insights.quote: The street of Armuse is still uh not uh free for navigation and there's still supply disruptions uh over there.

insights.claim: Yardeni flags as flippant the White House claim (which he attributes to Scott Bessent) that within two years the Strait of Hormuz won't matter, arguing it is still disrupting oil supplies now.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Policy complacency on energy chokepoints means the market may be underpricing duration of the oil supply risk.
insights.quote: I think um was it Scott Bessent who recently said that in within two years this won't this the straight of Hormuz won't matter

insights.claim: The quiet period in the Iran conflict may be a setup for a major attack rather than de-escalation, with Iran threatening to hit US allies in the region if attacked again.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
entities: US allies in the Middle East
insights.so_what: Tail risk of a regional escalation that would spike oil and hit risk assets is not resolved by the current calm.
insights.quote: it's possible that all this quiet is a setup for a major attack on Iran
